summary: "Suurvaras" by J. Blicher-Clausen is a novella written in the early 20th century. Set in rural Jutland, it probes how slander—the theft of a person’s good name—corrodes lives and communities. The narrative centers on the embittered veteran doctor Horn and his principled young successor Dr. Höjstrup, with Horn’s foster daughter Inger as the story’s moral and emotional pivot. The opening of the novella frames its theme by contrasting countless “small thieves” with the single true “great thief”: the stealer of reputation. In a remote district, Dr. Horn sells his practice yet schemes to keep lucrative cases, greets the idealistic Höjstrup with covert hostility, and quietly spreads doubts about him, even as the newcomer wins the poor through tireless, compassionate care and refuses to gossip. When an apothecary’s child faces a life‑or‑death crisis and Höjstrup is briefly away, Horn withholds a recall telegram, has a groom break into Höjstrup’s locked instrument cabinet, performs the operation with the stolen tools, and basks in the parents’ praise. Inger confronts him, calling this a moral theft akin to profaning the altar; soon after, Horn is struck on his right side and left partially disabled. Höjstrup returns ready to denounce him, but on learning of the stroke, tempers justice with compassion. Horn resumes a brittle social charm as an invalid while Inger cares for him dutifully yet coolly, and the section closes with Höjstrup pressing on through oppressive heat to serve patients, underscoring his resolve amidst lingering tensions.
